extracted.intended_audience: patent practitioners, patent litigators, USPTO/PTAB attorneys, and IPO members
extracted.subtask_description: Analysis and comparison of the Broadest Reasonable Interpretation (BRI) and Phillips claim construction standards as applied in USPTO proceedings (prosecution, reexam, IPR/PGR/CBM) and in district court litigation, including related procedural doctrines (estoppel, burden of proof, effect of expiration).

rubrics_metrics.name: BRI claim construction standard
rubrics_metrics.description: The BRI standard requires consideration of the “broadest reasonable meaning of [a claim’s] words in their ordinary usage as they would be understood by one of ordinary skill in the art, taking into account whatever enlightenment by way of definitions or otherwise that may be afforded by the written description contained in the applicant’s specification.” Claim words are given their ordinary and customary meaning unless the patent applicant acts as his own lexicographer. The PTO should also consult the prosecution history. While extrinsic evidence is not prohibited, it should be considered secondarily and in a limited manner so that the interpretation is the broadest reasonable interpretation, not just the broadest interpretation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Applied by the USPTO in pre-issuance examinations and most post-issuance review proceedings (e.g., traditionally in reexams and AIA trials). Cannot be divorced from the specification and record evidence (Microsoft v. Proxyconn; In re NTP). Cases show the Board/Examiners may interpret terms more broadly under BRI; however, the Board should avoid importing improper limitations from the specification (Papst-Motoren). Examples: PTAB constructions under BRI in PPC Broadband and other PTAB decisions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Phillips claim construction standard
rubrics_metrics.description: Under Phillips, claims are given their ordinary and customary meaning — “the meaning that the term would have to a person of ordinary skill in the art in question at the time of the invention.” Primary reliance is placed on intrinsic evidence (claims, specification, prosecution history); extrinsic evidence is secondary.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Applied by district courts following the Federal Circuit’s en banc Phillips decision. Phillips reconciled earlier inconsistent precedent (Vitronics, Texas Digital) and clarified intrinsic-evidence-first approach. USPTO has proposed (and in some circumstances adopted) applying Phillips in PTAB proceedings for expired patents or by rulemaking (proposed rule 83 Fed. Reg. 21221).

rubrics_metrics.name: Inventor acting as lexicographer (definitional safety valve)
rubrics_metrics.description: An inventor can act as his own lexicographer by defining specific terms “with reasonable clarity, deliberateness, and precision” such that he ‘set[s] out his uncommon definition in some manner within the patent disclosure’ so as to give one of ordinary skill in the art notice of the change in meaning.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When applicants explicitly define terms in the specification, that definition governs under both BRI and Phillips. Under BRI, decision makers may be less forgiving if owners have not clearly acted as lexicographers. See In re Paulsen and Intellicall precedent quoted in the text.

rubrics_metrics.name: Intrinsic evidence primary; extrinsic evidence secondary
rubrics_metrics.description: Both BRI and Phillips emphasize primary reliance on intrinsic evidence (claim language, specification, prosecution history) to construe claim terms, with extrinsic evidence (dictionaries, expert testimony) considered only secondarily.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Under BRI extrinsic evidence is allowed but limited and subordinate to intrinsic evidence to ensure the interpretation is the broadest reasonable one. Phillips likewise places extrinsic evidence secondary to intrinsic sources. See Phillips, Vitronics discussion, and PPC cases where specification usage controlled.

rubrics_metrics.name: BRI cannot be narrower than Phillips (relative breadth principle)
rubrics_metrics.description: The broadest reasonable interpretation of a claim term may be the same as or broader than the construction of a term under the Phillips standard. But it cannot be narrower.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is summarized in Facebook v. Pragmatus and applied in post-grant litigation: if a PTAB/BPAI construction under BRI is narrower than a Phillips construction, that may be erroneous. Use this as a sanity check when comparing constructions across forums.

rubrics_metrics.name: Application contexts for each standard (procedural rule placement)
rubrics_metrics.description: Historically the USPTO applied BRI during prosecution and most post-grant proceedings, while district courts apply Phillips. The USPTO (by rule or in practice) may apply Phillips for patents that will expire prior to the Office’s final decision or in specified circumstances (37 C.F.R. § 42.100(a); proposed rulemaking 83 Fed. Reg. 21221).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Know which forum and timing govern choice of standard: pre-issuance and many USPTO proceedings → BRI; district courts → Phillips; expired patents in PTO appeals/IPRs → PTO may apply Phillips. Cuozzo affirmed USPTO authority to use BRI in IPRs absent rule change. Be alert to Director discretion and specific regulations or proposed rule changes that can alter application.

rubrics_metrics.name: Effect of patent expiration on claim construction
rubrics_metrics.description: When a patent expires during the pendency of a USPTO proceeding or appeal, the USPTO has sometimes applied a Phillips-type or district-court-type standard instead of BRI; cases show mixed results — in some instances a new (narrower) construction followed expiration, in others the construction remained the same.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Papst-Motoren and Ex parte Bowles (BPAI changed construction on expiration and reversed rejections); Rambus (examiner agreed to apply Phillips but found same construction); several PTAB/Federal Circuit cases where expiration led to different treatment. Check MPEP §2258.G and 37 C.F.R. §42.100 for rules on expiration handling.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid importing limitations from the specification (no wholesale reconstruction)
rubrics_metrics.description: Decision makers are warned against ‘wholesale reconstruction of the claims by importing limitations into the claims from the specification.’ Importing improper ‘inferential limitations’ from the specification into claims is barred (Papst-Motoren and In re Priest).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Both PTO and courts must be careful not to read limitations from the specification into claim language; whether a construction imports limitations is a key battleground and can determine outcomes under either standard. Cite examples where BPAI reversed examiner or affirmed rejections based on this principle.

rubrics_metrics.name: Presumption of validity (forum-dependent)
rubrics_metrics.description: District court proceedings treat patents as presumed valid. The PTAB and USPTO proceedings (e.g., IPRs, reexaminations) do not afford a presumption of validity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The absence of a presumption at the PTO may make PTAB proceedings or reexams more likely to find claims unpatentable. Empirical/experimental studies (e.g., Jeremy W. Bock) suggest the presumption affects validity findings (increase from ~24.7% to ~31.7% in mock juries). Consider presumption when assessing comparative risk of invalidity in PTO vs district forums.

rubrics_metrics.name: Standard of proof for invalidity (evidentiary standard)
rubrics_metrics.description: The PTAB uses a preponderance-of-the-evidence standard to invalidate claims (35 U.S.C. §316(e)), whereas district courts require clear-and-convincing evidence for invalidation (Microsoft v. i4i).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Empirical work (Schwartz & Seaman) shows different invalidation rates under the two standards (e.g., 38.3% under preponderance vs 27.1% under clear-and-convincing in experiments). This difference, together with the presumption of validity, contributes materially to different outcomes between PTO and courts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Collateral estoppel (issue preclusion) prerequisites and limits
rubrics_metrics.description: Collateral estoppel applies if four prerequisites are met: (1) the issue decided in the previous proceeding is identical to the one sought to be relitigated; (2) the issue was actually litigated in the prior proceeding; (3) the determination was a critical and necessary part of the judgment on the merits in the first proceeding; and (4) the party against which estoppel is asserted had a full and fair opportunity to litigate the issue in the first proceeding.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because PTAB applies BRI and courts apply Phillips, the Federal Circuit has held that collateral estoppel does not automatically oblige the PTAB to follow a district court’s Phillips construction (In re Trans Texas). If both fora use Phillips, collateral estoppel is more likely to bar relitigation, subject to regional circuit law on finality and exceptions (B & B Hardware, Trans Texas, SkyHawke). Consider appeal status and whether the prior decision is immune to reversal before asserting estoppel.

rubrics_metrics.name: Judicial estoppel (doctrinal factors)
rubrics_metrics.description: Judicial estoppel precludes a party from taking a later position clearly inconsistent with an earlier one where (a) the later position is clearly inconsistent, (b) the party persuaded a court to accept the earlier position (so acceptance would create the perception the court was misled), and (c) the party would derive an unfair advantage or impose unfair detriment on the opponent if not estopped.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Parties should avoid flip-flopping between broad and narrow constructions across tribunals; courts have penalized inconsistent litigation positions (e.g., Source Search Tech. fee award). Judicial estoppel considerations apply even when different claim-construction standards are used, but are particularly salient if both PTAB and courts apply the same construction standard.

rubrics_metrics.name: Director discretion and management of parallel USPTO proceedings
rubrics_metrics.description: The Director has statutory authority (e.g., 35 U.S.C. §315(d)) to determine how to proceed when a patent is involved in multiple USPTO proceedings (IPR, reexam, reissue, derivation). The Director may choose to institute, stay, or decline institution to avoid inconsistent outcomes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical options include not instituting an IPR where a reexam is pending, staying reexam, or otherwise coordinating proceedings to limit application of different claim-construction standards across concurrent USPTO proceedings. This discretion can reduce occasions for inconsistent constructions within the Office.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of prior court constructions by the USPTO (not strictly bound)
rubrics_metrics.description: The USPTO is not strictly bound by district-court claim constructions, though examiners and the Board may adopt or rely on prior court constructions; the Office has sometimes chosen to follow a court’s narrower construction but has noted that it is not bound to accept it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: examiners in Guardian Media and Katz reexams accepted prior court constructions (but noted lack of binding effect); BPAI and PTAB sometimes adopt district-court constructions when persuasive. Expect the PTO to treat prior court rulings as informative but not determinative unless rule or regulation requires otherwise.

rubrics_metrics.name: Predictability and fact-specificity of outcomes under BRI vs Phillips
rubrics_metrics.description: Differences in outcomes under BRI and Phillips are fact-specific and hinge on how aggressively the decision maker reads claims in light of the specification and how close that reading comes to importing limitations. The same claim term may be construed the same under both standards or may differ; empirical and case-law evidence shows both possibilities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: No simple rule reliably predicts which standard will yield broader or narrower construction for a given term. Practitioners must analyze claim language, specification usage (e.g., repeated use of a term to mean encircle), prosecution history, and forum-specific incentives (presumption, burden) to assess risk. Case examples: PPC Broadband (standards outcome-determinative), Rambus and Straight Path (constructions similar despite different standards).
